query: Consider the following context: Non-equiatomic high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are promising candidates for low-dimensional magnetocaloric applications. In that context, which method can be used for tuning the magnetic and magnetocaloric behavior, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Systematically varying the alloy composition of non-equiatomic HEAs via combinatorial synthesis can tune their magnetic ordering and magnetocaloric response by modifying the electronic and magnetic exchange interactions.
generation.material_initial_state: Non-equiatomic high-entropy alloys prepared as a single-phase, random solid solution.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled compositional gradient using combinatorial synthesis methods to systematically adjust the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Synthesis under controlled processing conditions that allow for precise tuning of elemental concentrations, followed by magnetic characterization at temperatures relevant for low-dimensional magnetocaloric applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Local changes in atomic arrangement and electronic structure induced by composition variation.
generation.mechanism: Variation in elemental ratios alters the electron concentration and tunes magnetic exchange interactions, which in turn affects both magnetic ordering and the magnetocaloric effect.
generation.predicted_outcome: A systematic change in the alloy composition will lead to measurable shifts in the magnetic transition temperatures and an optimized magnetocaloric effect (e.g., enhanced isothermal entropy change), potentially improving the performance for low-dimensional magnetocaloric applications.
generation.baseline: Non-equiatomic HEAs with nominal composition synthesized without intentional compositional gradients.
generation.boundary: The tuning effect may be limited if excessive composition changes lead to phase separation or secondary phases, which can obscure the magnetocaloric behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the magnetic and magnetocaloric improvements is uncertain and may vary with the specific HEA system and processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of non-equiatomic HEA samples with a controlled compositional gradient using combinatorial synthesis. Evaluate the phase composition using XRD and assess the magnetic properties (e.g., magnetization versus temperature, and isothermal entropy change) using VSM or SQUID magnetometry over the relevant temperature range.
measurements: Magnetization measurements via VSM or SQUID
Calorimetric assessment of isothermal entropy change
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the systematic variation in composition does not result in consistent and measurable shifts in magnetic ordering or magnetocaloric properties, or if the observed changes are attributed solely to the emergence of secondary phases rather than optimized single-phase behavior, the hypothesis should be considered falsified.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted a lot of attention in recent years, due to the unique combinations of structural, physical and chemical properties of these alloys [1] – [3] . HEAs usually form simple structures such as body-centered cubic (BCC) (e.g. TaNbHfZrTi [4] , NbTaVWZr [5] etc.) or face-centered cubic (FCC) (e.g., CoCrCuFeNi [6] , CoCrFeMnNi [7] etc.) solid solutions. The large number of the alloying elements in near-equiatomic proportions result in high configurational entropy in these solid solutions. However, these alloys can decompose to multiple phases upon changing the composition or annealing at different temperatures or a combination of both [8] – [10] . Such a phase decomposition is often the result of the complex interplay of configurational entropy of mixing with the enthalpies of mixing of the constituent elements. Additionally, such multiphase microstructures are more likely to exhibit the desired properties for real engineering applications. Hence, tuning the composition and fractions of phases is critical for achieving the desired properties [10] , [11] .

High entropy alloys (HEAs), complex concentrated alloys (CCAs), and multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) are the most common names of a new group of materials [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] ] introduced by Yeh et al. [ [6] ] and Cantor et al. [ [7] ] in the beginning of this century. Many definitions were proposed for such materials, but in general they consist of multiple (usually at least five) elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic composition [ [2] ]. This approach is different from the traditional alloy design using one (or maximum two) principal element and other minor elements. The presence of many elements in equiatomic (or near) composition leads to high mixing entropy and thus to many interesting properties [ [2] , [5] ]. One of such effects is the existence of a random solid solution and simple body centered cubic (bcc) or faced centered cubic (fcc) structure. Recently HEAs with hexagonal closed packed (hcp) structure have been reported as well [ [8] , [9] ]. A new approach to HEA design using the valence electron concentration (VEC) was recently proposed with the aim of increasing the plasticity of these alloys [ [10] , [11] ].
